title: Janoo Leads UNH’s Final Poll While Most of Its Respondents Expect Scott to Win - Compass Vermont
content: “Democratic newcomer Amanda Janoo holds a small lead over Republican incumbent Phil Scott in the race for Governor of Vermont. However, most likely voters in Vermont expect Scott to win.” That’s how the University of New Hampshire opened its final poll of the governor’s race, released Sunday. The poll has Janoo, a Democrat/Progressive, leading Scott 51% to 43% among likely voters. Janoo’s campaign emphasized that lead in a Monday release headlined “Janoo is Up Eight Points in Final Poll as Lead Over Five-Term Governor Grows.” But the same survey produced another striking finding. Sixty-two percent of likely voters expect Scott to win, while only 25% expect Janoo to. Even among Janoo’s supporters, 40% expect Scott to prevail. The poll tells two different stories: whom voters prefer, and whom they expect to win Tuesday. Pollsters usually lead by asking people whom they’ll vote for. The UNH poll also asked: “Regardless of your vote, which candidate do you think is most likely to win the 2026 election for governor?” A voter can support Janoo and still expect Scott to win. The first answer measures that voter’s own choice; the second measures that voter’s read of everyone else. And 62% expecting Scott to win is not a 62% chance that he will. The expectation question has a strong record. Economists David Rothschild and Justin Wolfers found that asking voters who will win forecast presidential elections more accurately than asking how they’ll vote. In an analysis of the 2014 elections, expectation questions missed half as many governor’s races as vote questions did. The researchers’ explanation is that people answering about expectations draw on what they know of their friends’ and family’s plans. That record gives voters’ expectations weight, but it doesn’t establish which question will prove more accurate in Vermont this year. In the UNH poll, the two questions point in opposite directions. In September, UNH had Janoo at 49% and Scott at 43%, with 6% undecided. This time, UNH added a follow-up question for undecided voters asking which way they lean. Those voters are called leaners. The 51%-to-43% figure includes them. UNH also reports the result without leaners, which is the version that matches September: Janoo 50%, Scott 42%. Janoo’s reported lead widened from six points to eight. In those directly comparable results, her support rose one point and Scott’s fell one point. Changes that small don’t, by themselves, establish that the electorate shifted. The undecided share fell from 6% to 2%. Over the same period, independent Brian Judd rose from 2% to 4%, and Freedom and Unity candidate Dean Roy picked up 1%. UNH’s bar chart is titled “With Leaners” over both its September and October panels. The September numbers didn’t include leaners. A footnote under the chart says so. UNH lists a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 points for likely voters. That figure applies to each candidate’s share, not to the gap between them. Pollsters adjust their raw results so the people who answered look like the state as a whole. That’s called weighting. A rough calculation that leaves out weighting puts the margin of error on the gap at about 5.5 points, and Janoo’s eight-point lead exceeds that estimate. But UNH says its published margins have not been adjusted for the uncertainty weighting adds. So the 5.5-point calculation doesn’t settle how precise the weighted result is. UNH’s headline on the Vermont poll reads “Blue Wave Lifts Janoo Over Scott in Vermont?” That suggests party is the reason for Janoo’s lead. The survey doesn’t establish that. Most of her supporters, 72%, say their vote is more for Janoo than against Scott, and 82% of those say it’s about her specifically. That doesn’t rule out a broader partisan pull, but it isn’t evidence of one either. UNH released its New Hampshire poll the same day under a plain headline: “Dems Lead in Federal Races, Governors Race Deadlocked.” Of the three pollsters in this story, UNH is the only one whose fall surveys have put Janoo ahead. State Navigate, Oct. 23–25, 1,752 likely voters: Scott 49%, Janoo 46%. Vermont Public, September: Scott ahead by 10 points. UNH’s final poll in 2024 had Scott 39 points ahead of Esther Charlestin. He won by nearly 52, about 13 points more than the poll showed. As Compass reported in September, polls and prediction markets have each missed in Vermont before, and neither decides the race. UNH’s poll draws from a panel of about 2,700 Vermont adults recruited at random by phone, text and mail. In September, Survey Center director Andrew Smith said that kind of panel is the same method used by Gallup, CNN and Pew. UNH weighted the sample by age, sex, education and region, and to Vermont’s 2024 election results. The sample’s recalled 2024 presidential vote, Harris 62% and Trump 31%, closely matches the actual result of 64% to 32%. The poll also finds conditions that favor a challenger this year: Only 20% of Vermonters approve of President Trump, the lowest in New England. Democrats are more engaged: 69% say they’re extremely interested in the election, compared with 59% of Republicans. Janoo is better liked than Scott, with 54% favorable to his 42%. 38% of Janoo’s supporters say they voted for Scott in 2024. That’s reported crossover, the kind of shift a challenger needs. Read in full, the UNH poll measures a close race two ways, and the two point in different directions: whom voters support, and whom they expect to win. The release’s presentation leans further than its numbers do, with a “blue wave” headline the survey doesn’t establish and a September chart labeled with leaners it didn’t have. “A poll in the homestretch isn’t what tells us we’re succeeding,” Janoo said in Monday’s release. She pointed instead to turnout at her campaign’s canvasses and its endorsements, and said the campaign would spend every second until the polls close getting out the vote. Scott’s campaign has argued that polls understate his support. After the September polls, spokesperson Emma Shouldice said that “public polling has always undervalued the Governor’s support.” As of Friday, nearly 140,000 Vermonters had already voted, according to the Secretary of State’s office. That’s nearly half the 292,000 ballots cast in Vermont’s 2022 general election. Polls are open until 7 p.m. Tuesday. News comes from the facts. Opinions should only come from you. content: Democrats have opened leads in the races for U.S. Senate and New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District in the final days before the election, according to the latest University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll. The poll, released Nov. 1, found Rep. Chris Pappas, D-NH, expanding his lead over former Sen. John E. Sununu, R-NH, in the race for U.S. Senate by four points. Former Portsmouth city councilor Stefany Shaheen, a Democrat, has expanded her lead over Republican businessman Anthony DiLorenzo by nine points. The poll also found the race for governor between Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington narrowing to a tie, although the poll notes most voters think Ayotte will win. The survey comes as polls across the country have found Democrats in the lead and pundits speculate about a “blue wave.” The president’s party typically loses seats in midterm elections. The poll surveyed 2,182 New Hampshire residents online from Oct. 27-31. It has a margin of error of +/-2.1%. In the final days of the election, the poll found Pappas leading Sununu 54% to 42%, up from 50% to 42% in September. It also found that while Pappas’s net favorability of -6 stayed the same since September, Sununu’s has declined from -5 to -18, with notable declines among Independents and Democrats. The drop is likely due to negative campaigning in the final weeks of the campaign, the poll said. Much of Pappas’s negative campaigning against Sununu has been connecting him to President Donald Trump. Sununu has sought to distance himself from the president but had received his endorsement earlier this year. The poll revealed that of Pappas supporters, 87% say their vote is to oppose Trump. “The Democratic Party has done an effective job making this election a referendum on President Trump,” the poll said. The House races also see Democratic leads: while Shaheen in September only had a four point lead over DiLorenzo, she now leads him 56% to 43%. Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-NH, has maintained a double-digit lead over her Republican challenger, Lily Tang Williams, 56%-41%. The governor’s race between Ayotte and Warmington has “tightened significantly in the past month,” the poll revealed. While Ayotte led Warmington 47%-43% in September, the poll this month found them locked at 48% each. Warmington’s increase in support came from Democrats coalescing around her: 92% of Democrats now say they support Warmington, up from 83% in September. Despite the closeness of the polls, 75% of Granite Staters think that Ayotte will win, including 59% of Democrats. But in the New Hampshire legislature, Democrats hold leads on the generic ballot for Executive Council, state Senate and state House; all leads that have grown since September. Over half (53%) of voters say they plan to vote for a Democrat for Executive Council, 54% say they plan to vote for a Democrat for state Senate and 51% say they plan to vote Democrat for state House. Due to the gerrymandering of the state legislature seats, poll director Andrew Smith said that Democrats generally have to win 54% of the vote to take the majority in the state Senate. Republicans currently control the Executive Council 4-1, the state House 211-170 and the Senate 16-8.

title: Final UNH Poll Shows Janoo With Lead Over Gov. Scott - Seven Days Vermont
content:
Democratic/Progressive gubernatorial candidate Amanda Janoo has an 8-point lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Phil Scott, according to the final poll of the campaign released on Sunday by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center. Conducted online between October 27 and 31, the Green Mountain State Poll surveyed 1,231 respondents. Of likely voters, 51 percent said they will or have voted for Janoo, while 43 percent say they will or have voted for Scott. The results include participants who said they are leaning toward a candidate, a category not included in previous UNH surveys. The poll’s margin of error is 2.8 percent. Independent Brian Judd received support from 4 percent of survey participants. One percent said they support Freedom and Unity candidate Dean Roy, a high school student. Fewer than one percent said they would vote for June Goodband, the Peace and Justice candidate. Despite the results, the survey found that 62 percent of likely voters believe that Scott will win the election. Only 25 percent of voters think Janoo will win, and 13 percent are unsure. Janoo is more personally popular than Scott, the survey found. Fifty-four percent of likely voters have a favorable opinion of the 39-year-old political newcomer, compared to 42 percent who have a favorable opinion of the governor. Among likely voters who identify as Democrats, 78 percent support Janoo and 20 percent support Scott. Among Republicans, 85 percent support Scott and 10 percent support Judd, the independent candidate, the survey found. An earlier poll from UNH, released in late September, showed that 49 percent of likely voters backed Janoo, compared with 43 percent for Scott. But a poll released by Vermont Public soon after had Scott up 10 points. The Vermont Public poll found that 16 percent of voters were still undecided. A State Navigate poll, released on October 27, showed Scott with a 3-point lead over Janoo. In the lieutenant governor’s race, Sunday’s Green Mountain State Poll shows Democratic challenger Molly Gray, who held the post from 2021 to 2023, with a comfortable lead over Republican incumbent Lt. Gov. John Rodgers. Among likely voters, 63 percent said they will or have voted for Gray, while 34 percent said they will or have voted for Rodgers. U.S. Rep. Becca Balint (D-Vt.) also holds a wide lead over Republican nominee Gerald Malloy, according to the Green Mountain State Poll. Sixty-six percent of likely voters, including those leaning toward a candidate, said they will or have voted for Balint while 31 percent said they will or have voted for Malloy. As of Friday morning, nearly 140,000 Vermonters had turned in their ballots, according to the Vermont Secretary of State’s Office. Polls are open on Tuesday until 7 p.m. Both Janoo and Scott are on the road on Monday in a final push before Election Day. title: Final UNH poll still finds Gov. Phil Scott trailing Democrat Amanda Janoo - WCAX
content:
BURLINGTON, Vt. (WCAX) - The final poll before Election Day shows Amanda Janoo ahead of Phil Scott in Vermont’s race for governor. Of likely voters polled, 51% say they have or will vote for Janoo, while 43% want Scott to return for a record-setting sixth term. Just over 1,200 people took part in the poll, which was conducted by the UNH Survey Center. “All the indications are that Amanda Janoo has run an effective campaign,” said Matt Dickinson, a Middlebury College political science professor. Dickinson said the new UNH polling numbers reveal just how close this contest could be between political newcomer Janoo and the incumbent Scott. If the Democrat pulls off the win, it would be historic. “We haven’t seen an incumbent governor defeated since 1962,” Dickinson said. The poll shows affordability and high taxes are top concerns for Vermonters. They are two issues Scott has campaigned on and made his top priorities for years. But Dickinson said the Republican’s time in office could be partly the reason Janoo pulled ahead by 8 points. “Voters don’t feel they’ve been solved,” Dickinson said. “The finger is getting pointed at Phil Scott. At least according to the polls, enough voters are considering an alternative in that top spot.” But Scott, commonly named the most popular governor in the country, still gets high marks here. “His approval ratings in this poll are still quite high. People like Phil Scott,” Dickinson said. But he said people are unhappy with policies coming out of Montpelier. Polls vary. Dickinson said they’re just a snapshot in time, and how they’re conducted makes a difference, too. Reporter Darren Perron: The governor said he doesn’t put much faith in UNH polling, saying, quote, ‘It’s been a flawed poll my entire political life. They never get it right.’ What do you say to that? Matt Dickinson: Well, he’s right, historically the UNH poll has overestimated vote totals for Scott’s opponents in the last two gubernatorial races and have done so by huge margins... It may be that UNH altered their polling methodology here and they’re getting it right. But you can understand why Scott wants to downplay these results. Dickinson said who is surveyed also affects polling results. This new poll skews younger. “Younger voters are disproportionately supporting Janoo, so depending on your assumption on younger voters, you come to different projections on who’s gonna win this race,” Dickinson said. Dickinson said this latest poll will motivate both campaigns to double down on their efforts to bring out their bases and to reach those persuadable voters who haven’t already voted. The previous poll released on Sept. 24 showed Janoo ahead by six points at 49% to 43%. Among the other recent surveys, a Vermont Public poll showed Scott leading by 10 points, 42% to 32%. title: Monday Memo: UNH Says Gov Race Tied. Campaign Pros Say ‘Meh.’ - NH Journal
content: The Monday Memo is a mix of reporting, rumors, analysis, and unkind comments compiled from various sources and provided for your entertainment and enlightenment each Monday. Reader discretion is advised. Surprised by UNH Survey Showing Tied Gov’s Race? Don’t Be. Like the swallows returning to Capistrano, or new revelations of antisemitic statements by Abdul El-Sayed, so it is with the last-minute University of New Hampshire Survey Center dump of a “poll” that gets lots of headlines before the election and is quickly forgotten afterward. According to the UNH Survey Center, with just a day to go in the campaign, the New Hampshire governor’s race is tied at 48% each for Gov. Kelly Ayotte and Democrat Cinde Warmington. This shocking result sent a shockwave through the state’s political circles. The survey also found former U.S. Sen. John Sununu losing to future U.S. Senator Chris Pappas by double digits at 54% to 42%. The survey found a similar margin in the NH-01 race (Shaheen 56%, DiLorenzo 43%). “Because it’s garbage,” one GOP campaign operative told NHJournal. The RealClearPolitics polling average has Ayotte leading the race by nearly nine points. Warmington has never led — or even been close — in the polling average. If Team Ayotte isn’t losing sleep over these numbers, perhaps it’s because the Democratic Governors Association still hasn’t acknowledged that Warmington’s even running. Or because the DGA has yet to give her a single dollar of support, which is why the current spate of TV ads is being paid for out of Warmington’s own pocket. Or maybe it’s because they remember the final UNH Survey of 2024: “Ayotte Holds Small Lead Over Craig in NH Governor’s Race.” That survey had Ayotte and former Manchester Mayor Joyce Craig in a margin-of-error race (Ayotte 48, Craig 44). The final result? Ayotte won by more than nine points. In 2022, it was “Senate & CD1 Too Close to Call in NH.” Sen. Maggie Hassan barely beat Republican Don Bolduc, 50% to 48%, while Rep. Chris Pappas fought for his political life against Karoline Leavitt, 50% to 49%; at least, according to UNH. Final number: Pappas won by eight and Hassan won by nine. And again in 2018: “NH Governor Race Too Close To Call,” with Chris Sununu and former state Sen. Molly Kelly tied at 46%. Final answer? Sununu by seven. UNH has also gotten some races pretty close, to be fair. They predicted big wins for Reps. Kuster and Pappas in 2018, and had Sununu way ahead in 2020 and 2022. Then again, an average Concord barroom drunk could have done the same. The point is, while the UNH number will get lots of clicks and plenty of press, New Hampshire campaign pros are shrugging it off. Dr. Smith’s survey operation may not be a Dartmouth College disaster (it had Craig leading Ayotte by 17 points in 2024), but its numbers aren’t enough to keep candidates up at night, either. Bow and arrow? Check. Horseback? Check. “Free Palestine?” Check. Rep. Ellen Read is a lock for reelection as a Newmarket state rep. Hey, how many of the other 399 could even get on a horse? Much less go full “Pocahontas” from the saddle? Why the horse, you ask? What does that have to do with serving as a state rep? You could ask the same question about “Free Palestine.” Some mean-spirited Republicans have suggested she’s on horseback because the courts have taken away her driving privileges, and she’ll soon be riding Seabiscuit to the State House. Not a chance. That’s the question Rep. Joe Sweeney, R-Salem, is asking about a series of mailers without the “paid for” disclaimers that are required by federal and state law that hit mailboxes last week. The mailers, which were sent by a Democratic print shop in Massachusetts, attack Republican John Sununu and boost third-party candidate Edmond Laplante. The attorney general has sent a cease-and-desist letter to the Journeyman Press and Pinpoint Campaigns, the two businesses responsible for the mailer. According to Sweeney, “the New Hampshire Democratic Party’s own campaign finance report shows the party paid (Pinpoint Campaigns) $58,437.43 for ‘Mailing Services’ this month.” He also says “Journeyman Press has taken 91 payments from New Hampshire Democratic committees and candidates since 2024.” Sweeney has posted these questions for the state Democratic Party and Chairman Ray Buckley: “Democrats are so desperate to stop John Sununu that they’re taking a page out of Mary Peltola’s book and trying to rig the election,” says the NRSC. If this story sounds familiar, it should. During the 2022 GOP primary in the 2nd Congressional District, illegal mail poured in to boost Bob Burns over popular Keene Mayor George Hansel. The mail was eventually traced back to the Democrats’ House Majority PAC in Washington, D.C. Several NHJournal readers have sent screen captures of this ad, which has popped up on their computer screens. Obviously it’s the wrong Sununu, but that’s not unusual. Hardly a day goes by when some national news anchor or debate moderator isn’t calling John “Chris.” Given the younger Sununu’s recent tenure as a popular four-term governor, and the 18 years since John last ran for public office, it’s an inevitable slip of the tongue. But what’s the deal with this ad? It’s been around for weeks, and it’s never been corrected. NHJournal would contact the alleged sponsors, the “Independence Project,” but they don’t exist. Go to the “Independence Project” website, and it’s a single, static image. No contact information, no explanation of why they’re running political ads. Maybe it’s just to annoy John E. Sununu, who is clearly bugged by the “Sunu-who?” issue. The NYTimes reports that Democrats have internal polling on the issue and “they say confusion abounds.” Chris Sununu has already given his answer. “Look, if people thought they were voting for me, my brother would be up by 30 points. Come on.” The New York Times reported last week that Alaska U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola knew about the conspiracy to find someone named Dan Sullivan and get him on the ballot to confuse voters hoping to vote for incumbent GOP U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan. That report has been confirmed by multiple sources, not least of which is that “Decoy Dan” has fled his home in the wake of the revelations. While Peltola may be running on the other side of the continent, the Alaska congresswoman has a close connection to New Hampshire’s Chris Pappas — close enough that they’ve sent joint fundraising emails. Now that Peltola’s been exposed for participating in this high-profile dirty trick, one designed to defraud voters, does Pappas still endorse her for U.S. Senate? Pappas declined to respond to multiple requests for comment after The New York Times reporting. Interestingly, Pappas also declined to respond when Graham Platner was his party’s nominee for U.S. Senate in Maine. Despite his Nazi tattoo, his anti-gay slurs, and credible charges of abusing women, Pappas would not condemn Platner’s statements or behavior until after it was clear the offensive oysterman was going to be off the ballot. Compare that to what Pappas’s fellow congressional Democrat, Haley Stevens, is doing in Michigan, standing up against the antisemitic, pro-Hamas U.S. Senate nominee of her own party. title: Voices of UNH Manchester Wildcats Series: Meet Mechanical Engineering Technology Major, Kieran McCurdy, '25 - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you considering a future in mechanical engineering technology? Meet Kieran McCurdy, class of '25 at UNH Manchester, whose journey offers a firsthand look at the value of this dynamic program. Whether you’re a prospective student or simply curious about what makes UNH Manchester stand out, Kieran’s experience highlights the unique opportunities, hands-on learning, and career advantages waiting for you. For Kieran, the decision to attend UNH Manchester was driven by the program’s practical focus and its strong industry connections. He shares, “UNH Manchester is a hub for all these different companies. When you graduate, there are all these job opportunities that you can go into.” The campus’s location in the heart of Manchester, NH, puts students close to leading engineering firms and tech companies, opening doors to internships, networking, and career placement right after graduation. Kieran’s experience in the mechanical engineering technology program is marked by a diverse curriculum and hands-on learning. He explains, “My favorite thing about the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester is the array of classes you take. I get to learn about thermodynamics, electrical, and mechanical stresses all in one degree.” This means students gain expertise across multiple engineering disciplines, preparing them for a wide range of careers. Classes at UNH Manchester teach students not only theory; they also show them how to apply their knowledge in real-world situations. Kieran notes, “I’m taking a 3D printing class. With this class, I’ve been able to level up my 3D printing skills because I’m able to think more critically about the way I design.” The program’s modern facilities, including advanced labs and equipment, further support this hands-on approach. Highlights from Kieran’s Mechanical Engineering Technology Journey One of the highlights of Kieran’s journey was the capstone project, where he worked alongside fellow students to build robots. He explains, “You work on a team with three to four engineers, and you’re building robots. You’re required to make three 3D printed parts per robot and three machine parts per robot.” The project culminates in a friendly competition that lets students test their creations and celebrate their achievements. This experience encourages teamwork, critical thinking, and practical problem-solving. Kieran’s time at UNH Manchester has been filled with opportunities to apply his skills in real-world settings. As an automation intern at Freudenberg, Kerian gained valuable exposure: "We had an inspection machine there. I worked on the wire diagram for that machine," he shares. These internships, made possible by the campus’s industry connections, help students build their resumes and prepare for the workforce. Beyond the curriculum, Kieran appreciates the small class sizes and the collaborative environment. Faculty are invested in student success, and peers share a passion for innovation and problem-solving. The campus’s supportive community and access to advanced technology make it an ideal place to grow as an engineer. Graduates of the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester often go into the following fields: As graduation approaches, Kieran is confident in his path. “After I graduate, I plan on working as a process engineer. I want to work at either BAE or DEKA because these are companies that are at the forefront and are located right next to UNH Manchester.” He credits the program for giving him the practical skills needed to succeed: “I got those practical skills that I need to work as a process engineer.” Watch and listen to Kieran's full story about his mechanical engineering technology journey at UNH Manchester and his career goals: Choosing UNH Manchester means choosing a campus that’s deeply connected to industry, offers hands-on learning, and supports your professional ambitions. BOSTON (WHDH) - Election Day is Tuesday and voters are set to voice their choice and in four of the biggest races we’re watching, we are seeing three candidates with big leads and one race that’s in a dead heat, according to our Exclusive 7NEWS/University of New Hampshire poll. In the race for governor in Massachusetts, Democrat Mauray Healey is looking to win another term against Republican challenger MIke Minogue. In our poll, Healey holds 55 percent of the vote, with Minogue getting 36 percent. Independent candidate Ashley James grabbed 4 percent. UNH Survey Center Director Andy Smith said President Trump is having a big impact on the race. “We’re seeing on our elections polling, not just in Massachusetts but across New England, is that Democratic voters are really excited and looking forward to going out to vote and every one of their votes is essentially a vote against Donald Trump. It’s going to be very difficult for him to peel off some of those voters,” he said. In the Massachusetts U.S. Senate race, Sen. Ed Markey leads attorney John Deaton by 21 points. We also polled likely voters in the Granite State about who they’re supporting in the New Hampshire U.S. Senate race. U.S. Congressman and Democrate Chris Pappas leads Republican and former Senator John Sununu by 12 points, 54 to 42 percent. Software developer Stephen Villee grabbed 2 percent of support. “It’s not really a race between Ayotte and Warmington … it’s really a race where the Democrats are going to come out and vote in that Senate race and they’re going to vote Democrat down that ticket,” he said. The University of New Haven is mourning the passing of a student after he was hit by a wrong-way driver. Ryan O’Shea, a senior criminal justice major and captain of the university’s club men’s ice hockey team died late Friday night after the car he was driving was struck by a wrong-way driver on I-91 in North Haven. The school said O’Shea interned with the New York City Police Department last summer, and hoped to start his career as a police officer after graduating. He aspired to work for the Drug Enforcement Administration one day. “Ryan was an avid sports fan, and he was always ready to have a sports-related conversation,” his academic adviser Lorenzo Boyd, Ph.D., Stewart Professor of Community Policing, said in a release. “Ryan wanted to go into public service in order to help others.
